questions.q: Per this lesson, when do you actually know your DR plan works?
options: Only after you've deliberately triggered a real failover and watched it complete, not simply because the mechanism was configured correctly
As soon as an Availability Group or geo-replication is configured, with no further verification needed
Only after a real, unplanned disaster has already happened once
As soon as the documentation for the DR plan has been written and approved
questions.explain: Configuration alone doesn't prove the plan works — issues like blocked firewall ports or stale connection strings only surface during an actual triggered failover.

questions.q: Besides confirming the failover itself completes, what else must a real failover test verify?
options: That the application reconnects, that data loss matches the expected RPO (not more), and that failing back to the original primary is also possible
Nothing else — confirming the failover completed is sufficient on its own
Only that the Azure bill for the secondary region is within budget
Only that the secondary database has a different name than the primary
questions.explain: A complete test checks reconnection, RPO accuracy, and fail-back — each is a separate way an otherwise-successful failover can still leave a real gap.

questions.q: What does a climbing log_send_queue_size or redo_queue_size in sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states indicate?
options: An early warning that a secondary replica is falling behind and needs attention before it becomes an outage
That the primary database has run out of storage space
That the Availability Group has already automatically failed over successfully
That the query itself has failed and returned no meaningful data
questions.explain: Growing queue sizes signal the secondary isn't keeping up with the primary — exactly the kind of early warning routine monitoring is meant to catch.

questions.q: What is the Azure SQL Database geo-replication equivalent of monitoring an AG's synchronization health, per this lesson?
options: Checking replication lag via the Azure Portal's failover group overview, or querying sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status on the primary
There is no equivalent monitoring available for Azure SQL Database's geo-replication
Manually pinging the secondary server's IP address every hour
Restoring a full backup on a schedule to confirm data is current
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database exposes the same lag/health concept through the Portal and sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status, just for Azure-managed infrastructure instead of a self-managed cluster.

questions.q: What comes immediately after Chapter 14 closes, and what does it actually consist of?
options: Chapter 15, Real-World Azure DBA Project — one continuous capstone scenario pulling together migration, security, performance, automation, and a disaster simulation
Chapter 14 restarts from Lesson 82 with harder difficulty
The course ends immediately after Chapter 14
Chapter 15 is an unrelated set of isolated topics with no connection to prior chapters
questions.explain: Chapter 15 is explicitly one continuous project tying together everything since Chapter 1, closing the loop by simulating a real disaster against the same environment.
